Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Utilities Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Utilities' Q3 2024 Earnings Call. Joining me on the call today are Mark Harlan, Chief Executive Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer; Tom Rivera, Chief Operating Officer, and Elena Vasquez, Chief Strategy Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that statements made during this call that are not historical facts are forward-looking statements and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied. Please refer to our SEC filings for a detailed discussion of these risks.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Mark Harlan.

Mark Harlan: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on our performance this quarter. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities, delivering solid results in a challenging environment.

Our performance was driven by strong operational performance in our generation fleet, continued growth in our renewable energy portfolio, effective cost management, progress on our infrastructure investments, and successful execution on our fleet repowering initiatives.

Let me provide some more detail on these five key aspects. First, on operational performance: we saw fleetwide capacity factors averaging 72% across thermal assets, with O&M expenses down 12% year-over-year to $285 million, thanks to predictive maintenance and digital twins that cut unplanned outages significantly.

Second, renewable growth: we announced the retirement of our 1,200 MW Springdale coal units and are advancing replacements like the 800 MW Lone Star Solar project paired with storage, positioning us for 85% carbon-free generation by 2030.

Third, cost management: we're actively mitigating regulatory lag, which impacted ROE by about 55 basis points this quarter, through formula rates, trackers, and multi-year rate plans that have narrowed the gap considerably.

Fourth, infrastructure progress: quarterly capex hit $1.4 billion, growing our rate base to $45 billion, with investments in transmission and renewables supporting data center load growth.

Fifth, repowering execution: we've retired or committed to 3,400 MW of legacy fossil assets since 2020, unlocking cost savings and deploying diversified replacements from solar to batteries and efficient gas.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa Chen to discuss the financials.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, Mark. Good morning, everyone. For the Q3 2024, we reported earnings per share of $1.42 and revenue of $4.75 billion. Our financial performance reflects the strength of our diversified business model and our disciplined approach to capital allocation.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q3 2024 earnings call for Apex Utilities. I'll walk you through our financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2024, with detailed comparisons to the prior-year quarter and the sequential second quarter, highlighting the key drivers across our regulated utility, competitive generation, and renewables segments. Then, I'll provide our updated full-year guidance and forward outlook. As always, these results reflect our disciplined execution amid a dynamic energy landscape marked by surging load growth from data centers and electrification, favorable capacity auction outcomes in PJM and ERCOT, and our ongoing transition to a cleaner, more resilient generation fleet.

Starting with the headline numbers: For Q3 2024, we delivered consolidated adjusted EBITDA of $1.28 billion, up 14% from $1.12 billion in Q3 2023 and up 8% sequentially from $1.18 billion in Q2 2024. GAAP net income came in at $425 million, or $1.42 diluted EPS, compared to $372 million or $1.24 EPS in the prior-year quarter—a 14% EPS growth—and $398 million or $1.33 EPS in Q2. Revenues totaled $4.75 billion, a robust 12% increase year-over-year from $4.24 billion, driven primarily by higher realized power prices and volume growth, partially offset by lower natural gas generation margins due to our strategic hedging. Sequentially, revenues rose 6% from Q2's $4.48 billion, reflecting seasonal cooling demand and stronger renewables output.

Let me break this down by segment to give you the full picture.

Regulated Utility Segment: This core cash cow generated $2.1 billion in revenues, up 9% YoY from $1.93 billion, and flat sequentially. Adjusted EBITDA here was $825 million, a 12% YoY increase from $735 million, thanks to authorized ROE recovery on our $15 billion rate base, which grew 7% YoY via $1.2 billion in capital investments during the quarter—primarily transmission upgrades to support PJM's RTEP queue for 20 GW of new data center interconnections. Rate base now stands at $45 billion, positioning us for another 6-8% organic growth in 2025. Weather was a tailwind: HDDs were 15% above normal in our Northeast territories, boosting residential and C&I cooling loads by 8%. Sequentially, margins held steady despite Q2's milder summer, as our dynamic pricing mechanisms captured peak demand pricing under FERC Order 2222 DER aggregation pilots.

Competitive Generation Segment: Here, we saw outsized growth, with revenues of $1.65 billion, up 18% YoY from $1.40 billion and up 10% from Q2's $1.50 billion. EBITDA jumped 22% YoY to $320 million from $262 million, fueled by elevated spark spreads—our NYMEX Henry Hub hedges locked in $3.25/MMBtu realization rates against $2.80 spot—and capacity payments from the PJM BRA auction, where our 4 GW gas fleet cleared at $270/MW-day, 25% above prior years. Nuclear uptime hit 93% capacity factor across our 2.2 GW fleet, up from 91% YoY, benefiting from post-Fukushima refits and extended license renewals mirroring those at Constellation Energy. However, coal retirements—we idled another 400 MW at our Midwest plants—dampened volumes by 5% YoY, aligning with our IRP commitments to MISO for net-zero by 2045.

Renewables and Storage Segment: This high-growth area delivered $1.0 billion in revenues, surging 22% YoY from $820 million and 5% sequentially, with EBITDA margins expanding to 45% from 42%. Key wins included 1.2 TWh of output from our 5 GW portfolio—solar at 28% capacity factor in ERCOT amid strong insolation, wind at 38% in the Plains, and our 1 GW BESS fleet discharging 450 GWh at $150/MWh arbitrage premiums during Texas heat domes. PPAs with hyperscalers like Amazon and Microsoft ramped to 85% contracted, capturing $60/MWh fixed prices plus uplift from LCFS credits under the IRA's Section 45X PTC. YoY, this segment's EBITDA doubled to $450 million from $225 million, driven by the commercial operation of our 500 MW SunWind hybrid project in California, which integrates bifacial panels with VPP software akin to Stem's Athena platform.

Corporate and Other: Opex came in at $2.9 billion, up 7% YoY due to $150 million in higher property taxes on new builds and $80 million in interest expense from our $10 billion green bond issuance at 4.8% yield. Capex totaled $1.4 billion in the quarter, on track for $5.2 billion FY full-year, with 60% allocated to renewables and grid hardening against extreme weather, as seen in Hurricane Helene's impacts on Southeast peers.

Now, turning to cash flow and balance sheet strength: Operating cash flow was $1.45 billion, up 16% YoY, supporting $650 million in dividends and $300 million in share repurchases under our $2 billion program. Liquidity remains robust at $4.2 billion, with net debt to EBITDA at 3.4x—well below our 4.0x target—and investment-grade ratings intact from S&P and Moody's.

Key Trends and Strategic Insights: Load growth is the story of the year—our territories saw 4.5% YoY retail sales growth, accelerating to 6% C&I from data centers alone, outpacing EIA forecasts and mirroring NextEra's experience. We've hedged 90% of our 2025 gas fleet exposure at $3.40/MMBtu and 85% of power sales at $55/MWh, insulating against volatility. Technically, our AI-driven forecasting—powered by Palantir-like tools—improved load prediction accuracy to 96%, optimizing dispatch and capturing $120 million in ancillary services revenues. Regionally, PJM's capacity crunch drove 30% auction price hikes, benefiting our Northeast assets, while ERCOT's voluntary generation adequacy metrics rewarded our BESS additions amid 15 GW of retirements. Strategically, we're ahead of the curve on decarbonization: 45% of our portfolio is now emissions-free, with $3 billion queued for 2 GW of new solar-plus-storage under the ADVANCE Act's transmission fast-track. This positions us to monetize IRA ITCs at 50% adders for domestic content, targeting 12-14% unlevered IRRs.

Updated FY2024 Guidance: Based on Q3 momentum and Q4 visibility—including mild weather assumptions, $55/MWh basin power prices, and 2% load growth—we are raising our full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to $5.10 - $5.25 billion, from $4.95 - $5.15 billion, implying 11-15% growth over FY2023's $4.60 billion. Diluted EPS guidance is now $5.60 - $5.80, up from $5.40 - $5.65. Capex remains $5.1 - $5.3 billion, with AFFO supporting a 4.2% dividend yield. For Q4, expect EBITDA of $1.35 - $1.45 billion, with renewables output +20% YoY.

Looking to 2025, we're framing initial thoughts around 10-12% EBITDA growth, anchored by 3 GW of CODs, rate case wins in two states, and $400 million in recurring capacity revenues. Risks include fuel volatility, regulatory lag on capex recovery, and supply chain delays for panels amid U.S. polysilicon tariffs—but our 18-month hedge runway and $2 billion development pipeline mitigate these.

Thank you, Mark, and good morning, everyone. Today, I'd like to dive deeper into one of our most transformative strategic pillars: the accelerated retirement of our legacy fossil fuel assets and our comprehensive replacement strategies. As you know, the U.S. power generation sector is undergoing a seismic shift, with coal capacity retiring at an average of 5 GW per year since 2020—up from 3 GW annually pre-2015—driven by EPA's Mercury and Air Toxics Standards, state-level carbon pricing in markets like RGGI, and plummeting renewable LCOEs. For Apex Utilities, this isn't just compliance; it's a $1.2 billion opportunity over the next five years to optimize our 25 GW portfolio, enhance reliability, and deliver superior risk-adjusted returns.

Let me start with the facts on our retirements. In Q3, we announced the full decommissioning of our 1,200 MW Springdale coal-fired units in the PJM market—assets averaging 55 years old with heat rates north of 10,500 Btu/kWh and annual O&M costs exceeding $45 million. These plants operated at just 35% capacity factor last year, burdened by $120/ton SO2 allowances and volatile coal prices spiking to $150/short ton amid supply chain disruptions. We'll shutter Springdale by Q4 2025, joining the retirements of our 800 MW Garrison gas peakers in ERCOT last year and the 400 MW legacy oil units in ISO-NE earlier this decade. Cumulatively, we've retired or committed to retire 3,400 MW of subcritical coal and simple-cycle gas since 2020—12% of our fossil fleet—unlocking $250 million in annual avoided fuel and emissions compliance costs.

This isn't haphazard; it's guided by our Fleet Optimization Model, which integrates NREL's Annual Technology Baseline data, EIA's AEO 2024 projections, and real-time ISO locational marginal pricing forecasts. In high-renewable penetration queues like MISO South, where we've seen 150 GW of renewables seeking interconnection, we're prioritizing brownfield repowering to bypass multi-year study delays.

Now, turning to replacements—our strategy is diversified, reliability-focused, and IRA-leveraged to achieve 85% carbon-free generation by 2030 and net-zero by 2045. We've allocated $2.8 billion in CapEx through 2028, fully funded via 4.5% blended financing from green bonds and tax equity partnerships.

Renewables Anchor (65% of Replacement Capacity): We're deploying 2,200 MW of solar-plus-storage across our footprints. In ERCOT, our 800 MW Lone Star Solar project—featuring 550 MWdc of bifacial TOPCon modules from LONGi at a record-low $0.75/Wdc—comes online Q1 2025, paired with 300 MWh of Tesla Megapack 2XL lithium-iron-phosphate systems for 4-hour dispatchable firming. This hybrid yields an LCOE of $28/MWh, 40% below the retired coal's $65/MWh all-in cost, bolstered by IRA's 30% ITC plus 10% domestic content adder. Capacity factor? Expect 28-32% with tracking, capturing Texas' solar irradiance peaks above 1,800 kWh/kWp annually.

In PJM, our 600 MW Appalachia Wind Farm—leveraging GE 6.1 MW turbines with 155m rotors—targets 45% capacity factor in the windy ridges, replacing Springdale's baseload void. We've secured a 15-year PPA at $35/MWh, hedging against negative pricing events that plagued 15% of ERCOT hours last summer.

Battery and Flexibility Bridge (25%): To maintain grid stability amid duck curve challenges in CAISO-adjacent markets and SPP, we're adding 1,200 MW / 4,800 MWh of standalone and co-located storage. Highlights include our 400 MW / 1,600 MWh Big Battery in MISO, using Form Energy's iron-air long-duration tech for 100-hour discharge—critical for winter storms like Uri 2.0. This fleet arbitrages 20% spreads between off-peak solar dumps and peak evening demand, generating $180 million in ancillary services revenue annually at PJM's RegD rates.

Firm Capacity and Transition Fuels (10%): No blind rush to intermittency. We're converting 500 MW of Garrison's gas footprint to a H-Class CCGT from GE Vernova, with 62% efficiency and hydrogen-ready blending up to 30%—aligning with DOE's H2@Scale initiative. In the Northeast, we're exploring NuScale's 77 MW SMRs for ISO-NE baseload, with FERC pre-approval in our queue position #47.

Regional Nuances and Risks: Footprint matters. In coal-heavy SPP, retirements face just transition pushback—we've committed $50 million to workforce retraining via our Apex Green Jobs Academy, partnering with IBEW Local 270, mitigating 400 job losses. ERCOT's deregulation favors merchant upside, with our solar fleet capturing $50/MWh scarcity pricing 5% of hours. PJM's capacity auctions, however, demand black-start capable assets; our storage bids cleared at $155/kW-year RPM 2028/29. Weather-normalized, we're modeling 15% EPS accretion from these moves, with IRR >12% post-ITC.

Strategically, this positions us ahead of peers like Dominion Energy, which retired 2.4 GW coal but lags in storage queues, or NextEra, our JV partner on 1 GW offshore wind off Virginia via their Vineyard Wind model. Market tailwinds? Wood Mackenzie forecasts U.S. battery additions doubling to 25 GW by 2027, while coal's share dips below 15%. Risks—interconnection delays (average 4.2 years per LBNL)—are hedged via $300 million in transfer capability buys.

In sum, these retirements and replacements aren't just greenwashing; they're delivering 8-10% ROE uplift, rate base growth to $45 billion, and resilience for customers facing 4% annual load growth from EVs and data centers. We're not betting the farm on one tech—we're building a portfolio with 99.9% SAIDI reliability.

Thank you, Mark, and good morning, everyone. I'll now turn to our Operations and Maintenance, or O&M, expense management initiatives, which continue to be a cornerstone of our profitability and operational resilience here at Apex Utilities. As you know, in the Utilities and Power Generation sector, O&M typically represents 20-30% of total operating expenses, and with our diversified fleet—spanning 15 GW of combined-cycle gas turbines, 5 GW of nuclear, 8 GW of renewables, and supporting T&D assets—we've prioritized structural cost efficiencies to offset inflationary pressures like rising labor wages, supply chain disruptions, and volatile natural gas prices averaging $3.50/MMBtu in Q2.

Let me start with the headline numbers. For the quarter, consolidated O&M expenses came in at $285 million, a 12% year-over-year decline, or roughly $42 million below our prior-year run rate. This marks the third consecutive quarter of double-digit O&M reductions, bringing our trailing 12-month O&M as a percentage of revenues down to 18.2% from 22.1% a year ago—outpacing peers like NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy, who reported 8-10% improvements in their latest prints. On a per-MWh basis, we've shaved O&M costs to $14.20, a 14% drop, driven by higher fleetwide capacity factors averaging 72% across our thermal assets, up from 68% last year.

These gains aren't one-offs; they're the result of a multi-pronged strategy we've accelerated since our 2023 digital roadmap launch. First, advanced predictive maintenance and asset performance management. We've fully rolled out GE Vernova's Predix APM suite across 80% of our CCGT fleet, integrating IoT sensors for real-time vibration, temperature, and emissions monitoring. This has reduced unplanned outages by 28%, from 4.2% to 3.0% of scheduled runtime, saving $18 million in Q2 alone. For context, our heat rates improved by 1.8% to 7,420 BTU/kWh on gas plants—on par with top-quartile performers per Wood Mackenzie benchmarks—avoiding $12 million in excess fuel burn at current nat gas pricing.

Complementing this, we've deployed digital twins for our three nuclear units in the Midwest, modeled after Exelon's successful Calpine implementation. Using Siemens' Xcelerator platform, these virtual replicas simulate degradation in steam generators and reactor vessel heads, enabling condition-based maintenance that cut refueling outage days by 15% this cycle. Result: $15 million in deferred capex and O&M, while maintaining NERC reliability standards with SAIDI at 85 minutes, below the U.S. average of 115.

On the renewables side, efficiency gains are powering our clean energy pivot. In ERCOT, our 2.5 GW wind portfolio—bolstered by Vestas V150-4.2 MW turbines—saw O&M per MW drop 22% to $28k through automated blade cleaning drones and AI-driven curtailment optimization amid record data center loads from hyperscalers like Google and Microsoft. This countered Q2 wind curtailments, which hit 15% regionally due to grid congestion, yielding $8 million in avoided losses. Similarly, in CAISO, our 1.8 GW solar-plus-storage hybrid (with 800 MWh of Tesla Megapacks) benefited from proprietary battery degradation algorithms, extending cycle life by 12% and trimming O&M to $22k/MW—well below Enphase and First Solar averages.

Workforce and supply chain initiatives rounded out the quarter. Our "Skills 4.0" upskilling program, partnering with Deloitte, trained 1,200 field technicians on AR/VR for substation repairs, reducing labor hours by 18% and overtime by 25%. This is critical in high-cost regions like PJM, where union wages rose 6% YoY, but our total labor O&M fell 9% through attrition management and zero-based budgeting. On procurement, we locked in 70% of 2025 fuel via fixed-price swaps at $3.20/MMBtu—hedging against Henry Hub volatility—and bulk-purchased transformers post-2022 shortages, saving $10 million versus spot pricing.

Regionally, performance varied but trended positive. Northeast PJM ops saw a 10% O&M cut despite FERC-mandated reliability investments, thanks to our shared transmission savings pool with PSEG and Exelon. In Texas ERCOT, weatherization post-Uri—$50 million in hardening for our gas peakers—paid off with zero weather-related derates in Q2 heatwaves. Southeast SERC assets benefited from nuclear uprates, adding 150 MW capacity with minimal incremental O&M.

Strategically, these initiatives position us for the IRA's clean energy tailwinds and the AI-driven load boom—projected at 15% CAGR per EIA. We're targeting another 10-12% O&M reduction in FY25, with $150-175 million in run-rate savings, half reinvested in battery dispatch optimization for ancillary services revenue. This not only bolsters our 9-11% EPS growth guidance but fortifies free cash flow to $1.2 billion, supporting our 4.5% dividend yield and $500 million buyback.

Of course, forward-looking statements are subject to risks like commodity prices and regulatory changes—please see our 10-Q for details.

Thank you, Mark, and good morning, everyone. As we dive into our Q3 results, I want to spend a few minutes addressing regulatory lag—one of the perennial challenges in our regulated utility business—and the proactive strategies we're employing to mitigate its impact on our earnings and returns. For those less familiar, regulatory lag refers to the time gap between when we deploy capital for essential investments—like grid hardening, renewables integration, and advanced transmission infrastructure—and when those costs are incorporated into our rate base and recovered through customer rates. This lag compresses our earned ROE below authorized levels, typically creating a 40-60 basis point headwind quarter-over-quarter, depending on the jurisdiction.

In Q3, regulatory lag shaved approximately 55 basis points off our consolidated regulated ROE, bringing our trailing 12-month earned ROE to 9.2% against an average authorized ROE of 9.8% across our footprints. Year-to-date, we've invested $2.7 billion in capital expenditures, with about 65% flowing into rate base—strong recovery, but the remaining $950 million is sitting in construction work in progress, accruing AFUDC at around 7.5%. This mirrors industry trends we've seen at peers like Duke Energy and Southern Company, where post-COVID supply chain disruptions and inflation have stretched construction timelines, exacerbating lag in states with traditional rate case cycles.

Let me break this down regionally, as our diversified footprint across PJM, MISO, and ERCOT gives us a unique lens. In the PJM zone, where we serve 4.2 million customers, our last base rate case settled in late 2023 with a $1.2 billion capex rider for transmission upgrades, including 500 kV reconductoring to support data center load growth—now forecasting 15 GW of new demand by 2028. However, $450 million of recent investments in battery storage and DERMS are pending FERC formula rate updates, expected Q2 2025. This has created a 70 bps lag here, but our forward-looking test-year methodology has accelerated recovery to within 9-12 months post-in-service.

Shifting to MISO Midwest, our formula rate mechanism—similar to Xcel Energy's—has been a game-changer, with annual clean-up filings allowing 85% true-up of O&M and capex variances. We've recovered 92% of our $800 million renewables spend YTD, including 450 MW of hybrid solar-plus-storage projects under our Clean Energy Transition Rider. Lag here is minimal at 20 bps, thanks to the forward test-year structure that captures inflation on steel towers and Siemens Gamesa turbine blades.

ERCOT, our unregulated merchant exposure arm, presents a different dynamic—about 20% of our generation mix. Post-Winter Storm Uri, we've hardened 1,200 miles of transmission with synchrophasors and drone-enabled inspections, but Texas PUC approvals lag traditional states. Our pending rate case, filed in August for $1.8 billion in grid resilience capex—including 300 MW of Form Energy iron-air long-duration storage—targets ROE recovery by mid-2025. Merchant hedges at $45/MWh for our 2 GW gas fleet have offset 30% of the lag, with implied heat rates improving 5% YoY via GE Vernova's fleet optimization software.

Now, turning to our mitigation playbook, which has narrowed lag by 25% since 2022. First, accelerated rate mechanisms: We've secured multi-year rate plans in two states, akin to PG&E's, locking in $3.5 billion over five years with quarterly earnings tests to minimize true-up delays. Our renewables tracker—mirroring NextEra's—recovers 80% of LevelTen PPA-adjusted costs pass-through, shielding 70% of our 1.2 GW solar additions.

Second, technological initiatives for capex efficiency: Deploying ABB's grid automation and Oracle's AI-driven load forecasting has cut outage-related deferrals by 15%, qualifying more assets for CWIP recovery. In pilot with NREL, our VPP platform aggregates 50 MW of customer-sited batteries, earning performance-based ratemaking incentives that boost ROE by 50 bps.

Third, financing innovation: Issued $1.5 billion in green bonds at 4.8%—below our 6.2% cost of equity—paired with $600 million in tax equity flips for wind farms, reducing equity outlay by 40%. This preserves rate base growth at 6-7% CAGR through 2027.

Strategically, we're advocating for lag-reducing reforms: Testifying before NARUC for nationwide adoption of forward test-years and decoupled ratemaking, while collaborating with EEI on IRP modernization to align capex with net-zero mandates like California's 90% clean by 2035. Looking ahead, we expect $2.4 billion in rate case recoveries next year, lifting earned ROE to 9.6% by year-end 2025, with lag stabilizing at 30-40 bps as 85% of our $10 billion five-year capex plan hits rate base.

In summary, while regulatory lag remains a drag, our multi-pronged approach—formula rates, trackers, tech, and advocacy—positions us for superior recovery versus peers.

Our capital expenditure for the quarter was $1.4 billion, primarily focused on renewables and transmission upgrades. We remain committed to maintaining a strong balance sheet and returning value to shareholders. We anticipate continued momentum into 2025 with 10-12% EBITDA growth.

Tom Rivera: Thank you, Lisa. Let me provide an update on the operational front. We are seeing improved efficiency in our combined-cycle gas power plants due to the implementation of GE Vernova's Predix APM suite. This has resulted in a 28% reduction in unplanned outages, translating to an 8% increase in overall output while holding SAIDI reliability below industry averages.

Elena Vasquez: Thank you, Tom. Turning to our long-term strategy, we are actively exploring opportunities in the long-duration energy storage space, including iron-air technologies and hydrogen-ready CCGTs. We believe this will be a key driver of future growth, ensuring grid stability as renewables scale.

Mark Harlan: Thank you, Lisa, Tom, and Elena. Now, we'll open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Julien Dumoulin-Smith with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith, BofA: Thanks, everyone. Strong quarter on the top line—beat on revenue and EBITDA. But can you walk us through the drivers behind the 14% YoY growth in adjusted EBITDA to $1.28 billion, particularly the merchant gas fleet performance in ERCOT amid those heatwaves? And any color on forward hedging for nat gas exposure?

Mark Harlan: Julien, great question. Yes, Q3 adjusted EBITDA came in at $1.28 billion, up 14% YoY, driven by a mix of regulated rate base growth and merchant upside. Breaking it down: our regulated utilities segment contributed $825 million, up 12% from base rate hikes and ROE recovery on our $45 billion rate base. But the star was merchant power gen, delivering standout performance.

In ERCOT, our 4.2 GW gas fleet—primarily CC assets like the 1,200 MW equivalents—posted a fleet-wide capacity factor of 68%, versus 52% last year, thanks to sustained heat domes pushing system lambdas above $200/MWh for extended hours. Real-time prices spiked high during peak stretches, and our peakers cleared at 95% availability. We captured robust spark spreads, with gross margins expanding significantly.

On hedging: We're 85% hedged for the back half at $35/MWh fixed, with collars on the remainder averaging $28 floor/$55 cap. Forward curve suggests $32/MWh winter strip, so we're comfortable with 20-25% merchant exposure. No major unwind risks—our fuel hedging book locks in Henry Hub at $3.10/MMBtu through 2025.

Operator: Next question from David Arcaro with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Arcaro, MS: David Arcaro, Morgan Stanley. On the renewables side, you announced 800 MW of new solar PPAs with hyperscalers—congrats. But with queue delays, how are you thinking about storage co-locates and battery dispatch economics in CAISO and PJM? Any updates on your 2.5 GW development pipeline IRR?

Lisa Chen: Thanks, David. Renewables were a bright spot: 1.4 GW added to our backlog, including those 800 MW solar + 200 MWh BESS deals with Microsoft and Google, at 12-year terms and $45/MWh fixed escalation. Total renewables EBITDA hit $450 million, up substantially YoY, with PTC/ITC extensions boosting after-tax yields.

Pipeline stands at 2.5 GW utility-scale solar/wind/storage across PJM, MISO, and CAISO. IRRs hold at 9-11% unlevered, with storage pushing the high end—our 100 MW/400 MWh pilot at the Rio Sol project in CAISO is arbitraging duck curve peaks, dispatching at $150/MWh+ during 4-9pm NETAs. Queue positions improved: PJM Stage 2 clearance for 600 MW, shaving interconnection costs by 20% via Energize study's network upgrades.

Strategically, we're targeting 50/50 solar/storage ratios going forward—LCOE now sub-$30/MWh blended. Regional note: CAISO's resource adequacy mandates are tailwinds, but NEM 3.0 headwinds are offset by our C&I direct PPAs.

Operator: Our next question is from Neal Dingmann with SunTrust. Please go ahead.

Neal Dingmann, SunTrust: Neal Dingmann here. Nuclear fleet utilization was impressive at 93%—kudos on synergies. With the IRA's nuclear PTC and SMR buzz, thoughts on restarts or new builds? And capex guidance—still $5.1-5.3B for '24?

Mark Harlan: Neal, spot on—our 3.2 GW nuclear fleet ran at 93.2% capacity factor, generating strong EBITDA. O&M costs down 8% to $12.50/MWh via shared services—mirroring models where we're involved. Zero refueling outages dragged positive.

Nuclear renaissance is real: IRA's zero-emission PTC at $18/MWh base (inflation-adjusted to $27/MWh '25) flips P&L on older units. We're evaluating two Palisades-style restarts: 1.1 GW mothballed fleet in the Midwest, targeting $45/MWh all-in costs post-PTC. SMRs? Early innings—partnered with NuScale on a 300 MW FOAK in MISO, queue position #47, IRR ~10% at $65/MWh PPA. But CCUS retrofits on gas first—$50M pilot capturing 90% CO2 for EOR.

Capex: Affirming $5.1-5.3 billion for '24—55% grid hardening, 30% renewables queue deposits, 15% nuclear life extensions. '25 guide $4.8B+, funding data center load growth—already 500 MW contracted in key zones.

Operator: Question from Stephen Byrd with Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead.

Stephen Byrd, DB: Thanks. Data center megatrends—how much of your backlog is hyperscaler-tied? Risks from AI power crunch delaying PPAs? And any Texas freeze-up learnings applied to winter storm prep?

Lisa Chen: Stephen, data centers are 40% of our 15 GW commercial backlog—3,200 MW firm, including 1.2 GW with Amazon in Northern Virginia (PJM) and 900 MW in Texas (ERCOT). Hyperscalers like NVDA-driven AI are committing 10+ year terms at $60-80/MWh, with escalation. Total load growth: PJM forecasts 2.5% CAGR to 2030, but data centers alone add 5 GW near-term.

Risks? Minimal—co-location PPAs with behind-the-meter BESS mitigate grid delays. We've got 1 GW shovel-ready, with interconnection deposits posted.

Winter prep: Post-Uri, our ERCOT fleet added 200 MW TAIs and 50 hours thermal storage. Drills show 99% survivability—nat gas firm transport at 1.2 Bcf/d secured.

Operator: Final question from Angie Storozynski with C.L. King. Please go ahead.

Angie Storozynski, C.L. King: Angie Storozynski. FERC Order 2020 compliance—impact on your SPP/MISO queues? And FY24 EPS guide—any raise with the beat?

Mark Harlan: Angie, FERC 2020 is reshaping queues—our 1.8 GW SPP cluster cleared Phase 1 modeling, but $250M in upgrades shared across 12 devs. MISO's similar: 900 MW wind/storage now at 12-month study. Net: $100M capex add, but accelerates 2027 CODs.
